questions.enonce_markdown:
He is referred to as "Ideal Israel" :

*Options as printed:* A) Esau   B) Isaac   C) Jacob   D) Abraham
questions.corrige_markdown:
Jacob was renamed Israel after he wrestled at Peniel (Genesis 32), and the nation of Israel and its twelve tribes descend from him, so the nation bears his name. In course manuals "Ideal Israel" is a label for Jacob, the patriarch in whom the people of Israel is embodied. Esau is his twin brother, Isaac his father and Abraham his grandfather, and none of them received the name Israel. The label "Ideal Israel" is not a biblical phrase, so the key rests on the manual usage.

**Intended answer: C (Jacob).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: The event that forced Abraham to go down to Egypt was :
questions.corrige_markdown: Genesis 12:10 says that there was a famine in the land of Canaan, so Abram went down to Egypt to live there for a while. Nothing in the account mentions war, pagan women or idol worship as the reason for the journey. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: "The silent Patriarch". This refers to:
questions.corrige_markdown: Isaac is called the silent patriarch because the Book of Genesis records very few of his words and deeds compared with his father Abraham and his son Jacob: he is mostly shown as the obedient son (Genesis 22) and as a man who repeats his father's actions (Genesis 26). Jacob is the most active of the patriarchs, Esau is not a patriarch, and Samuel lived centuries later as a judge and prophet. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: The historical event that took place at Peniel was:
questions.corrige_markdown: At Peniel (Penuel), by the river Jabbok, Jacob wrestled with a mysterious figure until daybreak and was given the name Israel (Genesis 32:22-32); he named the place Peniel because he had seen God face to face. Esau's name was never changed to Israel, and Joseph did not have a theophany there. The meeting and reconciliation with Esau comes in Genesis 33, after Peniel, so it is not the event of Peniel itself. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

choix.texte: the changing of Jacob's name to Israel
the changing of Esau's name to Israel
the reconciliation between Jacob and Esau

questions.enonce_markdown:
It was where the Israelites first grumbled during the Exodus :

*Options as printed:* A) At Mount Sinai   B) At Rephidim   C) At the Red Sea   D) At Marah
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the wilderness the Israelites went three days without finding water; at Marah the water was bitter, the people grumbled against Moses, and the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood that made the water sweet (Exodus 15:22-25). Marah is the place usually taught as the first grumbling about the hardships of the desert journey. At Rephidim they quarrelled over water later (Exodus 17), and at Mount Sinai the sin was the golden calf (Exodus 32), not grumbling. At the Red Sea the people also complained to Moses out of fear of the Egyptian army (Exodus 14:10-12), so the word "first" makes the question open to discussion.

**Intended answer: D (At Marah).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown: What event made the Israelites to worship a golden calf ?
questions.corrige_markdown: While Moses stayed on Mount Sinai receiving the Law, the people saw that he was taking a very long time to come down and asked Aaron to make gods for them; Aaron fashioned the golden calf (Exodus 32:1-4). It was Moses who was delayed, not Aaron, who was in the camp, nor Joshua, who had accompanied Moses. The text does not say that the instructions were too hard. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown: The first war the Israelites fought in the desert was against :
questions.corrige_markdown: At Rephidim the Amalekites attacked Israel, and Joshua led the men in battle while Moses held up his hands on the hill with the help of Aaron and Hur (Exodus 17:8-16). The Perizzites, Canaanites and Jebusites were peoples living in the land of Canaan, whom Israel met later in the conquest. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown: He was the successor of Moses :
questions.corrige_markdown: God told Moses to commission Joshua son of Nun, who had served him and had spied out Canaan, and Joshua led Israel into the promised land after the death of Moses (Numbers 27:18-23; Deuteronomy 34:9; Joshua 1). Aaron was Moses' brother and high priest and died before him, Joseph lived centuries earlier and Manasseh was a son of Joseph. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - joshua and the conquest

questions.enonce_markdown: Samuel played the following three roles in Israel :
questions.corrige_markdown: 1 Samuel presents Samuel as a prophet recognised from Dan to Beersheba (1 Samuel 3:20), as a judge who judged Israel all the days of his life (1 Samuel 7:15) and as a priest who ministered before the Lord and offered sacrifices (1 Samuel 2:18; 7:9). He anointed the kings Saul and David but never reigned himself, so "king" is wrong in options A and B, and "saviour" is not one of his roles in option C. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: All were reasons for the institution of the monarchy in Israel except :
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1 Samuel 8 the elders of Israel asked Samuel for a king because Samuel was old, because his sons Joel and Abijah took bribes and perverted justice, and because the rule of the judges had not given Israel lasting security against its enemies; they wanted to be like the other nations. The disobedience of Saul cannot be a reason for the institution of the monarchy, since it happened after Saul had become the first king (1 Samuel 13 and 15). **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

choix.texte: The corrupt nature of Samuel's sons

questions.enonce_markdown: Saul committed all these sins except:
questions.corrige_markdown: The account of Saul reports that he offered the sacrifice at Gilgal instead of waiting for Samuel (1 Samuel 13:8-14), that he disobeyed Samuel and the command about the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15), and that he set up a monument for himself at Carmel (1 Samuel 15:12), which the question calls a statue. The Bible does not accuse Saul of marrying foreign wives: that sin is attributed to Solomon (1 Kings 11). **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

choix.texte: He made a statue of himself

questions.enonce_markdown: David transgressed against the following three Commandments :
questions.corrige_markdown: In the affair of Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11-12) David desired another man's wife, which is covetousness, he slept with her, which is adultery, and he arranged the death of her husband Uriah the Hittite in battle, which is murder. The prophet Nathan confronted him with this. Stealing and lying are not the main sins named in the narrative, so only option C lists the three commandments broken. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - david and the united kingdom

questions.enonce_markdown: One of these is the way Solomon consolidated the nation of Israel:
questions.corrige_markdown: Solomon divided the kingdom into twelve administrative districts, each under an officer responsible for providing food for the royal household for one month of the year (1 Kings 4:7-19); this replaced the old tribal boundaries and tied the tribes to the central government. He did not reduce taxes: the heavy taxes and forced labour led to the revolt after his death (1 Kings 12). He expanded rather than reduced trade partners. Solomon did keep many chariots, but the reorganisation into districts is the way usually taught as his method of consolidating the nation. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

choix.texte: Increased the size of the army

questions.enonce_markdown: Ahab's sin that led Elijah to oppose him was :
questions.corrige_markdown: Ahab married Jezebel of Sidon, built a temple and an altar for Baal in Samaria and encouraged Baal worship in Israel (1 Kings 16:29-33); this idolatry is what brought Elijah's announcement of drought and the contest with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 17-18). Ahab's later guilt in the affair of Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21) involved covetousness and murder, but the sin that first set Elijah against him was idolatry. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: He was more of a miracle-worker than a prophet :
questions.corrige_markdown: Elisha, the successor of Elijah, is remembered for a long series of miracles: the oil of the widow, the son of the Shunammite woman, the healing of Naaman and the axe head that floated (2 Kings 2-8). Nathan and Jeremiah are known above all for their spoken messages, and Elijah, although he also worked miracles, is the great prophetic confronter of Baal worship. Elisha is therefore the prophet described as more of a miracle-worker. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: The persecuted prophet who fled to Egypt was :
questions.corrige_markdown: Jeremiah was persecuted throughout his ministry: he was beaten and put in the stocks, thrown into a cistern and accused of treason (Jeremiah 20, 37-38). After the fall of Jerusalem the remnant of the people took him with them to Egypt (Jeremiah 43:5-7), where his ministry ended. Isaiah, Hosea and Amos are not reported to have gone to Egypt. Strictly speaking Jeremiah was carried there rather than fleeing, but he is the only prophet among the options linked with Egypt. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: The message of Amos is centred on :
questions.corrige_markdown: Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa who prophesied in the northern kingdom in the eighth century BCE, condemned the oppression of the poor, dishonest trade and the corruption of the courts, and called on Israel to let justice roll down like waters (Amos 2:6-7; 5:24). His message is therefore centred on social justice, together with the warning that ritual worship without justice is rejected by God. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: The peculiarity of the Jerusalem Temple was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Solomon built the Temple in Jerusalem as the dwelling place of the name of the Lord (1 Kings 6-8). Its distinctive character is that, after the centralisation of worship (Deuteronomy 12), it became the one legitimate place where Israel offered sacrifices. It was also a house of prayer, but not "solely" so, and it was neither a school nor a centre of international trade. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

choix.texte: It was the centre for learning
A place for offering of sacrifices

questions.enonce_markdown: Buddha's sermon at Benares after enlightenment was called :
questions.corrige_markdown: After his enlightenment the Buddha gave his first sermon to five ascetics in the Deer Park near Benares (Sarnath). It set out the Middle Way, the Four Noble Truths (suffering, its cause, its end and the path) and the Eightfold Path, and is known as the sermon on the Noble Truths (the printed option reads "Nobe"). The farewell teaching belongs to the end of his life, and the Sermon on the Mount is a teaching of Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: It was a strong quality of Theravada Buddhism :
questions.corrige_markdown: Theravada, the way of the elders, teaches that each person must achieve liberation by his or her own effort, following the Buddha's example, with no creator god or saviour to rely on. Salvation by grace and the ideal of the bodhisattva (the being who delays his own entry into nirvana to help others) belong to Mahayana Buddhism; the Theravada ideal is the arhat. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

choix.texte: Man is on his own in the universe

questions.enonce_markdown: The teachings of the Buddha are called:
questions.corrige_markdown: The teaching of the Buddha is called the Dhamma (Pali; Dharma in Sanskrit). Anatta means "no self", one of the three marks of existence, Bhikkhu means a Buddhist monk, and Dukkha means suffering or unsatisfactoriness, the subject of the first Noble Truth. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: Who is Brahman to the Hindus ?
questions.corrige_markdown: In Hindu thought Brahman is the ultimate reality: the eternal, infinite source and ground of everything that exists, which the Upanishads describe as beyond ordinary description. It is therefore the ultimate being, and not a fallible, forsaken or incarnate (the printed option reads "incarate") being. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: The belief in Hinduism that after death, the soul transfers to a new body is called :
questions.corrige_markdown: Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth in which the soul (atman) passes into a new body after death, according to its karma, until it attains moksha, liberation. Sarasvati is a goddess, Varuna a Vedic god and Yoga a discipline of spiritual practice. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: The most well-known of all Hindu scriptures is :
questions.corrige_markdown: The Bhagavad Gita, part of the epic Mahabharata, is the Hindu text most widely read and quoted; it records the teaching of Krishna to Arjuna on duty, devotion and knowledge. Agni is the Vedic god of fire, Brahman is the ultimate reality and Krishna is a deity, so none of these three is a scripture. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: The birth city of Mohammad is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Muslim tradition places the birth of Muhammad in Mecca, in the tribe of Quraysh, around 570 CE. Medina became his city of refuge after the Hijra in 622 CE, and Baghdad and Tehran were founded or became prominent much later. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: When Mohammad lost his mother, he was brought up by:
questions.corrige_markdown: According to the traditional biographies, Muhammad's father died before or soon after his birth and his mother Amina died when he was about six years old. He was then taken into the care of his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and, after the grandfather's death, of his uncle Abu Talib. The printed "Abu Multalib" is a distorted form of the grandfather's name, and it is the only guardian among the options. Khadija became his wife as an adult, and Abu Bakr and Umar were his companions and later caliphs. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: In Islam, the greatest event on " the night of glory" was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Night of Power or Decree (Laylat al-Qadr, called the night of glory in some translations, and the subject of Surah 97) is the night on which Muslims believe the first revelation of the Qur'an came to Muhammad through the angel Jibril in the cave of Hira, so the "vision" of option C is the event commemorated. The flight to Medina (Hijra) took place about twelve years later, and his death in 632 CE is not linked to that night. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

choix.texte: When Mohammad first saw his wife

questions.enonce_markdown: "The city of the prophet" in Islam refers to:
questions.corrige_markdown: Medina, formerly called Yathrib, received the name Madinat an-Nabi, the city of the Prophet, after Muhammad settled there following the Hijra of 622 CE. Mecca is his birthplace and the site of the Kaaba, while Mina and Arafat are places visited during the Hajj. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: Why did prophet Mohammad condemn excessive drinking?
questions.corrige_markdown: In Islam intoxicating drink is forbidden because it clouds the mind, leads to quarrels and neglect of prayer, and harms the individual and society; the Qur'an calls intoxicants a work of Satan to be avoided (for example in Surah 5, al-Ma'idah). Muhammad therefore condemned excessive drinking as a vicious act. Something virtuous would not be condemned, and the question does not rest on custom or primitiveness. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - social teachings of islam

choix.texte: Because it is a primitive act
Because it is a vicious act
Because it is a common act to people
Because it is a virtuous act

questions.enonce_markdown: He was the first successor of Prophet Mohammad:
questions.corrige_markdown: After the death of Muhammad in 632 CE the community chose Abu Bakr as the first caliph, and Sunni Muslims count him the first of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs, followed by Umar, Uthman and Ali. Shia Muslims hold that Ali should have been the immediate successor, but the account usually taught gives Abu Bakr as the first successor. Ibrahim was a son of Muhammad who died in infancy. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - rightly guided caliphs

questions.enonce_markdown: The title that was given to those who succeeded Mohammad was :
questions.corrige_markdown: The successors of Muhammad as leaders of the Muslim community were called caliphs (khalifa, meaning "successor" or "deputy"). Imam is the title Shia Muslims give to their divinely guided leaders and also names the prayer leader, while Sunnis and Shiites are names of the two main branches of Islam, not titles of office. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic community and leadership

questions.enonce_markdown: The testimony of faith in Islam is summarised in:
questions.corrige_markdown: The testimony of faith, the Kalima or Shahada, states that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God; it is the first pillar of Islam. Zakat (almsgiving) and Hajj (pilgrimage) are other pillars, and "Al-Ali" names nothing in the five pillars. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown: The largest Islamic sect :
questions.corrige_markdown: The Sunnis form the great majority of Muslims, usually estimated at 85 to 90 percent. The Shiites are the second largest branch, the Sophists were ancient Greek teachers and are not an Islamic group, and the Mu'tazilites were a rationalist school of theology of the early Abbasid period. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - sunni and shia origins

questions.enonce_markdown: It is the pillar in Islam that seeks to bridge the gap between the rich and the poor.
questions.corrige_markdown: Zakat is the obligatory almsgiving, normally calculated on savings and wealth held for a year above a minimum amount, and it is paid to the poor and needy. It redistributes wealth and narrows the gap between rich and poor. Sawm (fasting, printed "Sawn") teaches self-control and sympathy with the hungry, Hajj shows the equality of the pilgrims, and Salat is the daily prayer. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown: Why do Muslims celebrate the feast of "Eid-Ul-Adha "
questions.corrige_markdown: Eid al-Adha, the feast of sacrifice, falls on the tenth day of Dhu al-Hijja and recalls the willingness of Ibrahim (Abraham) to sacrifice his son at God's command, a trial for which God provided a ram instead (the story is told in Surah 37). In the Islamic tradition the son is generally identified as Ishmael (Ismail); some early scholars named Isaac (printed "Isiak"), but the Qur'an does not give the name and the usual Muslim teaching is Ishmael. The flight to Medina is commemorated by the Islamic New Year and the birth of the Prophet by the Mawlid. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - festivals in islam

choix.texte: To commemorate the sacrifice of Ishmael
To commemorate the sacrifice of Isiak
To commemorate Mohammad's flight to Medina
To commemorate the day Mohammad was born

questions.enonce_markdown:
What made Prophet Mohammad to turn from Jerusalem as the centre of worship to Mecca ?

*Options as printed:* A) Because his wife was in Mecca   B) Because Mecca was his birth city   C) Because there were more Muslims in Mecca   D) Because Jews and Christians rejected him and his teachings
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Medina, about a year and a half after the Hijra, the direction of prayer (qibla) was changed from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Mecca (Qur'an, Surah 2). In the usual account the change followed the refusal of the Jews of Medina to accept Muhammad and his message, together with his own wish to pray towards the house built by Ibrahim and Ismail, which is why options B and D can both be argued. The reasons in options A and C are not found in the traditional accounts, since Muhammad's wife Khadija had died before the Hijra and most Muslims were by then in Medina.

**Intended answer: D (Because Jews and Christians rejected him and his teachings).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: How are the Surah's arranged in the Qur'an ?
questions.corrige_markdown: The 114 surahs of the Qur'an are arranged, apart from the short opening surah al-Fatiha, roughly by length, from the longest (al-Baqara) to the shortest, and not in the order of revelation or alphabetically. Option B states this principle, which has some exceptions. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - the quran in islam

choix.texte: Following the day each Surah was written.
By length -the longer in front, the shorter in back
The shorter in front, the longer behind
They are arranged in alphabetical order

questions.enonce_markdown: Who was Fatima to Mohammad ?
questions.corrige_markdown: Fatima (Fatima al-Zahra) was a daughter of Muhammad and of his first wife Khadija. She married Ali and was the mother of Hasan and Husayn. She was therefore neither a granddaughter nor a niece. The text of option D is not printed in the scan. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

choix.texte: His daughter with the first wife

questions.enonce_markdown: The Muslim crier who announces the hour of prayer is called :
questions.corrige_markdown: The muezzin (mu'adhdhin) calls the faithful to prayer with the adhan, traditionally from the minaret of the mosque. The imam leads the prayer, the caliph is a ruler, and Alhaji (printed "Alhadji") is the title of a Muslim who has made the pilgrimage to Mecca. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic worship and practices

questions.enonce_markdown: He is the author of the 13 Articles of Faith:
questions.corrige_markdown: Moses Maimonides (Rambam), the twelfth-century Jewish scholar and physician, formulated the Thirteen Principles of Faith, which became a standard summary of Jewish belief. Moses Mendelssohn was an eighteenth-century philosopher of the Jewish Enlightenment, and the other names printed are not the author of this creed. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: The Roman general who destroyed the city of Jerusalem in 70 AD was:
questions.corrige_markdown: In 70 CE the Roman army under Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian, captured Jerusalem during the Jewish revolt and destroyed the Temple. The printed "Tetus" is Titus. Alexander the Great was a Greek conqueror of the fourth century BCE, Philemon was the recipient of one of Paul's letters, and Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea who condemned Jesus. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown:
Another name for the feast of weeks is :

*Options as printed:* A) Pentecost   B) Passover   C) Holocaust   D) Shabuot
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Feast of Weeks (Exodus 34:22; Deuteronomy 16:10) is held seven weeks, fifty days, after Passover. In Hebrew it is called Shavuot (printed "Shabuot") and in Greek Pentecost, the name used in Acts 2, so options A and D both name the same festival. Passover (Pesach) is a different feast, and "Holocaust" refers to the persecution and murder of the Jews in the twentieth century, not to a feast.

**Intended answer: A (Pentecost).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Why is African Traditional Religion described as "Religions"?

*Options as printed:* A) Because there are many ancestors   B) Because there are many priests   C) Because there are many gods   D) Because there are many mediums
questions.corrige_markdown:
Scholars speak of African Traditional Religions in the plural because the continent has many peoples, each with its own beliefs, myths and practices, even though they share common themes. Among the options, the plurality of divinities (many gods) is the one most often given in manuals to explain the plural, whereas the numbers of ancestors, priests or mediums are not usually cited.

**Intended answer: C (Because there are many gods).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: To whom do divinities owe their origin in ATR ?
questions.corrige_markdown: In the classical descriptions of African Traditional Religion the divinities (lesser gods) are the agents or ministers of the Supreme Being: they are created by God or derive their power from him, and they serve as intermediaries between God and people. They do not originate from the living-dead (ancestors), nor from mediums or diviners, who are human specialists serving the divinities. This is a general description, and beliefs vary between peoples. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr supreme being and divinities

questions.enonce_markdown: ATR is different from other Religions because:
questions.corrige_markdown: African Traditional Religion has no written scripture or single founder: its beliefs are passed from one generation to the next orally, through myths, proverbs, songs, rituals and the teaching of elders. Most African peoples believe in a Supreme Being, so option B is wrong, and ATR is among the oldest religious traditions, not the latest. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Sacrifices are important in ATR because:
questions.corrige_markdown: In African Traditional Religion sacrifices and offerings are made to the Supreme Being, the divinities, spirits and ancestors, in order to thank them, to appease them when they are angry, to ask for their protection and to restore harmony after a wrong. Sacrifices are meant to avert misfortune and to preserve order in the community, the opposite of options B and C. This is a general description, and practices vary between peoples. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: How is death perceived in ATR ?
questions.corrige_markdown: In African Traditional Religion death is not the end of existence: it is a passage from the world of the living to the world of the spirits, where the deceased become living-dead and, if they lived well and received proper funeral rites, ancestors who continue to watch over their families. Option C states this fully, while "the end of life" and "annihilation" deny it and option B is incomplete since it does not say where the person goes. This is a general description, and beliefs vary between peoples. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
It is not an abode of the spirits in ATR

*Options as printed:* A) Shrines   B) Forest   C) Lakes   D) Human bodies
questions.corrige_markdown:
In African Traditional Religion spirits are believed to dwell in natural places such as forests, rivers, lakes, mountains and big trees, and in shrines built for them. Among the options, human bodies is the one the question treats as not being a permanent abode of spirits, although in cases of possession a spirit may temporarily speak through a medium; the key is therefore open to discussion. This is a general description, and beliefs vary between peoples.

**Intended answer: D (Human bodies).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Marriage in ATR is for :
questions.corrige_markdown: In African Traditional Religion marriage is a sacred duty whose first purpose is procreation: to have children who continue the family line and keep the community alive, and through whom ancestors are remembered. Companionship, solidarity and friendship are also valued, but they are secondary to the bearing of children. This is a general description, and practices vary between peoples. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr marriage and family

questions.enonce_markdown: All of these are specialist in ATR , except :
questions.corrige_markdown: The religious specialists of African Traditional Religion are living human beings with a recognised role: medicine men or healers, diviners, mediums, priests and rainmakers. The ancestors are the departed (the living-dead) and not living specialists, so they are the exception. This is a general description, and roles vary between peoples. **Answer: D.**
